Situation1: A family member has a significant event they want to share with everyone.
Expectation2: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation2: A friend who has just started assembling furniture asks for a quick video call because the instructions are confusing.
Story: I was sitting in the living room, the scent of freshly baked cookies lingering in the air, when my daughter called out, “Grandpa, can you come here? Jamie wants to show everyone his science project!” I could hear the excitement in my grandson’s voice, and I knew how much it meant to him for the whole family to be there. Just as I stood up, my phone buzzed. It was a message from Mark, my old friend. “Hey, any chance you could hop on a quick video call? I’m losing my mind with these furniture instructions. I really need your help.” I glanced at the family gathered in the dining room, waiting for me, and then at my phone, picturing Mark surrounded by scattered screws and planks, probably feeling overwhelmed and alone. My heart tugged in two directions—one part aching not to disappoint my grandson, the other knowing how much Mark relied on me in moments like this. I felt the weight of both expectations pressing down, unsure which way to turn.
